# CMS Comparison for Next.js/React/TypeScript

## Ease of Use Breakdown

### Contentful
- **Developer Experience**: 8/10 - Well-documented API, strong TypeScript support
- **Content Editor Experience**: 9/10 - Clean, intuitive interface with minimal learning curve
- **Setup Complexity**: 7/10 - Quick to start, but advanced configuration takes time
- **Best For**: Enterprise teams with complex content models

Contentful excels for larger projects where you need flexible content modeling and robust workflows. It offers a polished editorial interface but comes with higher pricing for advanced features.

### Sanity.io
- **Developer Experience**: 8/10 - Highly customizable with React-based editor
- **Content Editor Experience**: 8/10 - Customizable but requires some adaptation
- **Setup Complexity**: 6/10 - More configuration required for customization
- **Best For**: Projects needing custom editing experiences

Sanity stands out for its flexibility in custom editing interfaces. It's great when you need to tailor the CMS to specific workflows, but this customization comes with a steeper learning curve.

### Strapi
- **Developer Experience**: 7/10 - Self-hosted with good TypeScript support
- **Content Editor Experience**: 8/10 - User-friendly admin panel
- **Setup Complexity**: 5/10 - Requires server setup and maintenance
- **Best For**: Teams that need full control over their CMS infrastructure

Strapi offers full ownership of your CMS as it's self-hosted. Great for developers who want control but requires more maintenance and server management.

### DatoCMS
- **Developer Experience**: 8/10 - Developer-friendly with good Next.js integration
- **Content Editor Experience**: 9/10 - Simple, clean interface with good UX
- **Setup Complexity**: 8/10 - Quick to set up with minimal configuration
- **Best For**: Small to medium projects looking for quick implementation

DatoCMS offers perhaps the fastest path to a working CMS with Next.js. Its GraphQL API and modular blocks make content modeling intuitive.

### Payload CMS
- **Developer Experience**: 9/10 - Built with TypeScript and designed for developers
- **Content Editor Experience**: 7/10 - Clean but slightly more technical
- **Setup Complexity**: 6/10 - Easy for developers but requires self-hosting
- **Best For**: TypeScript-focused teams that want deep integration

Payload is built specifically with TypeScript in mind, making it particularly appealing for Next.js/TypeScript projects. The self-hosted nature gives you control but adds maintenance overhead.

## Overall Recommendation

- **Fastest to implement**: DatoCMS
- **Most WordPress-like experience**: Strapi
- **Best TypeScript integration**: Payload CMS
- **Most enterprise-ready**: Contentful
- **Most customizable**: Sanity.io

For a solo developer or small team just getting started with Next.js/React/TypeScript, I'd recommend DatoCMS for its balance of ease of use and features. If you prefer self-hosting for cost reasons, Strapi provides the most WordPress-like experience.

Would you like more specific information about any of these options or help with setting one up?

# Free & Self-Hosted CMS Options for Next.js/React/TypeScript

For free and self-hosted solutions that work well with Next.js, React, and TypeScript, here's a revised comparison:

## Strapi
- **Ease of Use**: 7/10
- **TypeScript Support**: Good native support
- **Community & Resources**: Large, active community
- **Customization**: Highly customizable through plugins and API
- **Setup Time**: 1-3 hours for basic setup

Strapi is the most mature free self-hosted option with a WordPress-like admin interface. It's completely free for self-hosting and offers a RESTful API and GraphQL support out of the box.

## Payload CMS
- **Ease of Use**: 8/10 (for developers)
- **TypeScript Support**: Excellent (built with TypeScript)
- **Community & Resources**: Growing, but smaller than Strapi
- **Customization**: Extremely flexible for developers
- **Setup Time**: 1-2 hours

Payload is built specifically with TypeScript in mind and offers deep customization. The free version allows unlimited users and content with all core features.

## Ghost (Headless Mode)
- **Ease of Use**: 8/10
- **TypeScript Support**: Good with community types
- **Community & Resources**: Well-established community
- **Customization**: More limited than other options
- **Setup Time**: 1 hour

While primarily a blogging platform, Ghost can be used as a headless CMS and is completely free when self-hosted.

## Directus
- **Ease of Use**: 7/10
- **TypeScript Support**: Good
- **Community & Resources**: Growing community
- **Customization**: Very flexible, database-first approach
- **Setup Time**: 2-3 hours

Directus is an "open data platform" that can function as a CMS. It's database-agnostic and has powerful customization options.

## Tina CMS
- **Ease of Use**: 8/10
- **TypeScript Support**: Excellent
- **Community & Resources**: Small but active
- **Customization**: Git-based with good developer experience
- **Setup Time**: 1-2 hours

Tina CMS is unique as it's Git-based and allows editing content directly from your Next.js site. The open-source version is free for self-hosting.

## Recommendation

For a free, self-hosted WordPress-like system for Next.js/React/TypeScript:

1. **Strapi** is your best bet if you want something that feels most like WordPress with a familiar admin interface and plugin system.

2. **Payload CMS** is ideal if TypeScript integration is your highest priority - it's built with TypeScript from the ground up.

Both require some server setup but have good documentation to get you started. Strapi has a larger community which means more resources and plugins available.

Looking at this Next.js API route file, the GET request endpoint would be:

**`GET /api/health`**

This is determined by the file path structure in Next.js App Router:
- The file is located at `app/api/health/route.ts`
- Next.js automatically maps this to the URL path `/api/health`
- The `GET` export function handles GET requests to that endpoint

So when you make a GET request to `http://yourdomain.com/api/health`, this code will execute and return a health check response showing the status of your web server, MongoDB, and ChromaDB services.

This is a common pattern for health check endpoints that monitoring systems, load balancers, or DevOps tools can ping to verify that all your application's dependencies are running properly.

chat_messages.text:
You can test the health endpoint in PowerShell using `Invoke-RestMethod` or `Invoke-WebRequest`. Here are a few ways:

## Method 1: Using Invoke-RestMethod (recommended)
```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:3000/api/health" -Method Get
```

## Method 2: Using Invoke-WebRequest for more details
```powershell
$response = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "http://localhost:3000/api/health" -Method Get
$response.StatusCode
$response.Content | ConvertFrom-Json
```

## Method 3: With error handling
```powershell
try {
    $result = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:3000/api/health" -Method Get
    Write-Host "Health Check Result:" -ForegroundColor Green
    $result | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
} catch {
    Write-Host "Error: $($_.Exception.Message)" -ForegroundColor Red
    Write-Host "Status Code: $($_.Exception.Response.StatusCode.value__)" -ForegroundColor Red
}
```

## Method 4: One-liner with pretty output
```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod "http://localhost:3000/api/health" | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
```

**Notes:**
- Replace `localhost:3000` with your actual server URL and port
- The `-Depth 5` parameter ensures nested objects in the response are fully displayed
- If your app runs on a different port, adjust accordingly (common ports: 3000, 8080, 5000)

The response should show the health status of your web server, MongoDB, and ChromaDB services.

try {

    Write-Host "Status Code: $($response.StatusCode)" -ForegroundColor Yellow
    Write-Host "Response Body:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
    $json = $response.Content | ConvertFrom-Json
    $json | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10
    
    # Check individual services

    Write-Host "Web: $($json.services.web.status)" -ForegroundColor $(if($json.services.web.status -eq 'healthy'){'Green'}else{'Red'})

}

The health check endpoint you showed me (`/api/health`) is **not being used** by that dashboard. The dashboard is getting its status information from somewhere else entirely - likely:

4. **External monitoring service** (like Datadog, New Relic, etc.)

1. **Check the dashboard's network requests** (F12 Developer Tools → Network tab)
2. **Look for other health/status endpoints** in your codebase
3. **Check if there's a separate monitoring configuration** file
4. **See if the dashboard connects directly** to MongoDB/ChromaDB

The health check code you showed me might be:
- **Unused/abandoned code** 
- **For a different purpose** (maybe CI/CD, load balancers, etc.)
- **Not yet integrated** with the dashboard

This is actually a common issue - multiple health check systems that aren't synchronized. Good catch on spotting this discrepancy!

- Then decide whether to remove it permanently

Not quite! The `[...nextauth]` is a special **dynamic route** in Next.js, so it actually handles multiple endpoints:

**`/api/auth/*`** - where `*` can be various NextAuth.js endpoints like:

- `GET/POST /api/auth/signin` - Sign in page/form submission
- `GET/POST /api/auth/signout` - Sign out
- `GET/POST /api/auth/callback` - OAuth callbacks
- `GET /api/auth/session` - Get current session
- `GET /api/auth/csrf` - CSRF token
- `GET /api/auth/providers` - Available auth providers

The `[...nextauth]` syntax means "catch all routes" under `/api/auth/`, and NextAuth.js internally handles routing to the appropriate functionality based on the specific path.

**You wouldn't typically test this directly** with PowerShell because:
1. It's designed for browser-based authentication flows
2. It handles complex session management, cookies, CSRF tokens, etc.
3. The authentication happens through forms and redirects

**Instead, you'd:**
- Visit `/api/auth/signin` in your browser to see the login page
- Use the web interface to log in
- Check `/api/auth/session` to see if you're authenticated

This is the authentication system that protects your `/api/admin/available-scripts` endpoint!

function AdvancedNavbar() {

            backdropFilter: isScrolled ? 'blur(10px)' : 'none',
            borderBottom: isScrolled

              : 'none',
            transition: 'all 0.3s ease'
          }}
        >
          <Container size="xl" py="md">
            <Group justify="space-between">

              </Group>
            </Group>
          </Container>
        </Box>
      )}
    </Transition>
  );
}

- Keep mobile experience simple with Drawer

I've created the theme/index.ts file for the Hello Commerce replica using Chakra UI 3.17. This implementation leverages the new `createSystem` approach which is a significant change from previous Chakra UI versions.

## Key Features of the Implementation

1. **Color System**
   - Implemented the primary Hello Commerce color palette (#0066CC primary, #263238 secondary, #CFD8DC accent)
   - Created semantic tokens for colors that work across light and dark modes

2. **Typography**
   - Set up a comprehensive typography system with responsive font sizes
   - Used system fonts matching Hello Commerce's clean design approach
   - Configured consistent line heights and letter spacing

3. **Spacing and Layout**
   - Implemented an 8px-based spacing system for consistency
   - Configured border radiuses and shadows for depth

4. **Component Recipes**
   - Used `defineRecipe` (new in Chakra UI 3.17) for Button, Card, and Input components
   - Created variants that match Hello Commerce's design language
   - Added custom sizes for responsive component sizing

5. **Global Styles**
   - Configured base styles for HTML elements
   - Set up responsive text sizes for headings

## How This Uses Chakra UI 3.17's Updated API

The implementation takes full advantage of Chakra UI 3.17's enhanced features:

1. **`createSystem` Instead of `extendTheme`**
   - The new approach provides better type safety and organization

2. **Component Style Recipes**
   - Uses `defineRecipe` which replaces the old components object approach
   - Provides better separation of concerns and more flexible styling options

3. **Enhanced Semantic Tokens**
   - More powerful token system for light/dark mode switching
   - Better organization of design intent (text.primary vs specific colors)

4. **Improved Global Styles**
   - Uses `defineStyle` for global style definitions

This theme file serves as a solid foundation for building your Hello Commerce replica. It provides all the necessary styling tokens, component recipes, and configurations to create a consistent and visually appealing interface. The semantic tokens make it easy to maintain and update the theme in the future while ensuring design consistency.

content.text:
MantineProvider
MantineProvider
provides a [theme object](/theming/theme-object/) context value, manages color scheme
changes and injects [CSS variables](/styles/css-variables/). It must be rendered at the root of your
application and should be used only once.
[Usage](#usage)
[MantineProvider props](#mantineprovider-props)
MantineProvider
supports the following props:
[theme](#theme)
Pass [theme object](/theming/theme-object/) override to theme
prop. It will be merged with the default
theme and used in all components.
[colorSchemeManager](#colorschememanager)
colorSchemeManager
is used to retrieve and set color scheme value in external storage. By default,
MantineProvider
uses window.localStorage
to store color scheme value, but you can pass your own
implementation to colorSchemeManager
prop. You can learn more about color scheme management in the
[color schemes guide](/theming/color-schemes/).
[defaultColorScheme](#defaultcolorscheme)
defaultColorScheme
value is used when colorSchemeManager
cannot retrieve the value from external
storage, for example during server side rendering or when the user hasn't selected a preferred color scheme.
Possible values are light
, dark
and auto
. By default, color scheme value is light
.
You can learn more about color scheme management in the [color schemes guide](/theming/color-schemes/).
[cssVariablesSelector](#cssvariablesselector)
cssVariablesSelector
is a CSS selector to which [CSS variables](/styles/css-variables/) should be added.
By default, it is :root
. MantineProvider
generates CSS variables based on given [theme override](/theming/theme-object/)
and cssVariablesResolver
, then these variables are rendered into <style />
tag next to your application.
You can learn more about Mantine CSS variables in the [CSS variables guide](/styles/css-variables/).
[withCssVariables](#withcssvariables)
withCssVariables
determines whether theme CSS variables should be added to given cssVariablesSelector
.
By default, it is set to true
, you should not change it unless you want to manage CSS variables
via .css
file (Note that in this case you will need to generate all theme tokens
that are not a part of the default theme on your side).
[deduplicateCssVariables](#deduplicatecssvariables)
deduplicateCssVariables
determines whether CSS variables should be deduplicated: if CSS variable has the same value as in default theme, it is not added in the runtime.
By default, it is set to true
. If set to false
, all Mantine CSS variables will be added in <style />
tag
even if they have the same value as in the default theme.
[getRootElement](#getrootelement)
getRootElement
is a function that returns the root application (usually html
) element to set data-mantine-color-scheme
attribute.
Default value is () => document.documentElement
which means that data-mantine-color-scheme
attribute will be added to <html />
tag. You can learn more about color scheme management in the
[color schemes guide](/theming/color-schemes/).
[classNamesPrefix](#classnamesprefix)
classNamesPrefix
is a prefix for components static classes (for example {selector}-Text-root
).
Default value is mantine
– all components will have mantine-
prefix in their static classes.
In this case (default classNamesPrefix
), [Text](/core/text/) component will have the following classes:
mantine-focus-auto
– global utility classm-3nrA4eL
– component class, usually a random string, with this class library styles are appliedmantine-Text-root
– component static class, part of[Styles API](/styles/styles-api/)
With classNamesPrefix
you can change only static class:
Now [Text](/core/text/) component will have the following classes:
mantine-focus-auto
–classNamesPrefix
does not impact global utility classes – it is static and cannot be changedm-3nrA4eL
–classNamesPrefix
does not impact library class – it is static and cannot be changedapp-Text-root
– component static class hasclassNamesPrefix
instead ofmantine
[withStaticClasses](#withstaticclasses)
withStaticClasses
determines whether components should have static classes, for example, mantine-Button-root
.
By default, static classes are enabled, to disable them set withStaticClasses
to false
:
[withGlobalClasses](#withglobalclasses)
withGlobalClasses
determines whether global classes should be added with <style />
tag.
Global classes are required for hiddenFrom

tags.

You can learn more about Mantine CSS variables in the [CSS variables guide](/styles/css-variables/#css-variables-resolver).

By default Mantine supports 5 sizes for spacing, radius and shadows: xs, sm, md, lg, xl. content.title: Can I use private CSS variables to style components? | Mantine
content.text:
Frequently asked questions and in-depth guides for Mantine

Private CSS variables start with --_, for example --_input-bd-focus. These variables are a part of internal Mantine API and are not intended to be used by end users. In most cases private CSS variables are used to reduce specificity of styles and make them easier to override. Absolutely not. Private CSS variables can be changed or removed in minor and patch releases without any notice. In this case, if you use private variables to style components, styles of your application will silently (no errors will be reported by any tools) break after update. Private CSS variables were implemented to reduce specificity of styles when :where selector was not widely available. Now when :where is supported by all major browsers private CSS variables will be removed over time in most components. Use regular styles instead.

.input { // ❌ do not use private CSS variables --_input-bd-focus: red; --_input-placeholder-color: red; } .input { // ✅ use regular styles &:focus, &:focus-within { border-color: red; } &::placeholder { color: red; } }Expand code

# What is a Source Map?

A source map is a file that creates a mapping between the original source code you wrote and the transformed or minified code that's actually running in the browser. Let me explain why they're important and how they work:

## Purpose of Source Maps

When you develop a modern web application, your original source code typically goes through several transformations before it's served to browsers:

1. **Transpilation**: Converting modern JavaScript/TypeScript to older JavaScript for browser compatibility (e.g., using Babel)
2. **Bundling**: Combining many source files into fewer bundles (e.g., using Webpack, Rollup, or Next.js's built-in bundler)
3. **Minification**: Removing whitespace, shortening variable names, and optimizing code size
4. **Compilation**: Converting higher-level languages (like TypeScript, SCSS) to JavaScript and CSS

The result is code that's optimized for browser performance but difficult for humans to read and debug.

## How Source Maps Help

Source maps solve this problem by:

1. **Mapping transformed code back to original source**: When you're debugging in browser dev tools, source maps allow you to see and interact with your original, readable code rather than the transformed version.

2. **Preserving line numbers and file structure**: Even if your original 100 files get bundled into one, source maps help maintain the connection to the original file structure.

3. **Enabling accurate error reporting**: When an error occurs, the browser can show you where the error happened in your original source code, not in the transformed version.

## How Source Maps Work

A source map is a JSON file with a `.map` extension that contains information about:

- The original file names
- The transformed file name(s)
- Mappings between positions in the transformed code and positions in the original code

For example, if you have a file `app.tsx` that gets transformed into `app.js`, you'd also have an `app.js.map` that helps developers trace back from `app.js` to the original `app.tsx`.

## In Your Next.js Application

In your console logs, you saw errors like:
```
GET /_next/static/chunks/app/UnstyledButton.module.css.mjs.map 404 in 36ms
```

This means:
1. The browser is looking for the source map for a compiled CSS module
2. That source map file doesn't exist (404 error)
3. This is likely because either:
   - Source maps weren't generated for those particular files
   - There's a configuration issue with how source maps are being generated

## Source Maps in Development vs. Production

- **Development**: Source maps are typically enabled by default to make debugging easier.
- **Production**: Often disabled or served separately to reduce bundle size and protect source code privacy.

## Should You Be Concerned?

These 404 errors for source maps are common in development and usually don't affect your application's functionality. They're just indicating that the browser is looking for mapping files to help with debugging, but can't find them.

If your application is working correctly otherwise, these can be safely ignored. If you want to resolve them, you can adjust your Next.js configuration as I mentioned in my previous response to either properly generate those source maps or disable source map generation altogether.

```

This is a request made automatically by Chrome DevTools. Chrome is checking for a specific configuration file that your application doesn't have.

### Why is it happening?
This is normal behavior when using Chrome DevTools. Chrome is looking for a configuration file in the `.well-known` directory, which is a standard location for "site-wide metadata."

No. This is not an error with your application, and you don't need to create this file. It's just Chrome checking if you have special DevTools configurations.

```

1. **Identify the component**:
   - The error is related to a component called `VisuallyHidden` used in your blog route
   - It's specifically looking for the CSS module source map

   - Look for a component named `VisuallyHidden` that's being used in your blog section
   - Check if it has an associated CSS module file (something like `VisuallyHidden.module.css`)

3. **Check the build configuration**:
   - This error suggests source maps might be configured inconsistently in your build process

## Tools for Tracing 404 Errors

1. **Chrome DevTools Network Tab**:
   - Open Chrome DevTools (F12 or Right-click → Inspect)
   - Go to the Network tab
   - Filter for "404" status codes
   - This will show you detailed information about each 404 request

2. **Next.js Debug Mode**:
   - Add the `--debug` flag when starting your Next.js app:
   ```

   ```

   - Check if you're using the latest version of the library

   ```

   };
   
   module.exports = nextConfig;
   ```

Your folder structure isn't ugly at all! You're comparing two different architectural approaches, and both are valid for different contexts.

The first structure you mentioned appears to be a **monorepo approach** where `backend/`, `frontend/`, and `common/` are separate applications or packages. This works when you have a separate backend API (maybe Express.js, Fastify, or similar) alongside your Next.js frontend.

Your structure follows the **Next.js App Router convention**, which is the modern, recommended approach for full-stack Next.js applications. Here's why your structure is actually well-organized:

**Your structure's strengths:**
- **App Router compliance**: Using `app/` directory with proper page routing
- **Route groups**: `(admin)` and `(site)` for logical separation without affecting URLs
- **API routes**: Properly nested under `app/api/`
- **Component organization**: Clear separation between layout and UI components
- **Type safety**: Dedicated `types/` directory
- **Utility separation**: `lib/` for database and utilities, `scripts/` for tooling

**The key difference:**
- The first structure separates frontend/backend into different applications
- Your structure is a **full-stack Next.js app** where the backend is built into Next.js API routes

**Your structure could benefit from these small improvements:**
```
├── app/
├── components/
├── lib/
│   ├── auth/          # Authentication logic
│   ├── db/            # Database (you have this)
│   ├── hooks/         # Custom React hooks
│   └── utils/         # General utilities
├── types/
└── config/            # App configuration
```

Your architecture is actually quite modern and follows Next.js best practices. The "backend/frontend" split only makes sense if you're building separate applications. For a full-stack Next.js SaaS app, your approach is spot-on.

# Troubleshooting Guide for Hello Commerce Mantine Errors

## Quick Fixes for Common Errors

### 1. Clear Next.js Cache
```bash
# Delete the .next directory
rm -rf .next

# Restart the development server
npm run dev
```

### 2. Reinstall Dependencies
```bash
# Delete node_modules and package-lock.json
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json

# Reinstall dependencies
npm install

# Start the development server
npm run dev
```

### 3. Check CSS Import Issues

Make sure you're importing Mantine styles only once in your app. Check that:

- `@mantine/core/styles.css` is imported only in `src/app/providers.tsx`
- No other files import Mantine CSS
- No duplicate CSS imports exist

### 4. Update next.config.js

```javascript
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  reactStrictMode: true,
  swcMinify: true,
  experimental: {
    optimizeCss: true,
  },
  // Disable source maps in development to avoid .map errors
  webpack: (config, { dev }) => {
    if (dev) {
      config.devtool = 'cheap-module-source-map';
    }
    return config;
  },
};

module.exports = nextConfig;
```

### 5. Add CSS Custom Properties Support

Create a `src/styles/globals.css` file:

```css
/* src/styles/globals.css */
:root {
  --font-inter: 'Inter', sans-serif;
}

html {
  color-scheme: light;
}

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0;
}
```

Then import it in your layout:

```tsx
// Add this import to src/app/layout.tsx
import '../styles/globals.css';
```

### 6. Verify Package Versions

Ensure you have compatible versions:

```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "@mantine/core": "^8.0.1",
    "@mantine/hooks": "^8.0.1",
    "@tabler/icons-react": "^2.42.0",
    "next": "^14.0.0",
    "react": "^18.2.0",
    "react-dom": "^18.2.0"
  }
}
```

### 7. Development vs Production Issues

If errors only appear in development:

```bash
# Try building for production
npm run build

# Run production build locally
npm run start
```

### 8. Browser Cache Issues

- Hard refresh: `Ctrl+Shift+R` (Windows) or `Cmd+Shift+R` (Mac)
- Open developer tools and disable cache
- Try in incognito/private mode

## Specific Error Solutions

### CSS Module Map Errors
These errors are usually caused by:
1. Conflicting CSS imports
2. Next.js cache issues
3. Development server not properly restarting

**Solution:**
1. Clear .next cache
2. Restart dev server
3. Check for duplicate CSS imports

### Chrome DevTools JSON Error
This error is harmless and can be ignored. It's Chrome looking for PWA configuration.

## If Problems Persist

1. Check browser console for additional errors
2. Verify all file paths are correct
3. Ensure TypeScript compilation succeeds
4. Check for conflicting dependencies

## Debugging Commands

```bash
# Check for TypeScript errors
npx tsc --noEmit

# Run ESLint
npm run lint

# Check bundle analysis
npm install -g @next/bundle-analyzer
ANALYZE=true npm run build
```

chat_messages.text:
I think you might be mixing up two different NASA programs! NASA used the **Apollo spacecraft** to land on the moon (1969), not the Space Shuttle. The Space Shuttle program (1981-2011) was for low Earth orbit missions.

For the **Apollo moon landings**, NASA used the **Apollo Guidance Computer (AGC)** - a revolutionary but incredibly primitive computer by today's standards. It had:
- About 4KB of memory
- Weighed 70 pounds
- Used integrated circuits (cutting-edge for 1960s)
- Had a simple keyboard and display interface

This was actually one of the first computers to use **integrated circuits** instead of individual transistors, making it much smaller and more reliable than the room-sized mainframe computers of the 1940s-50s.

The AGC was developed in the **early-to-mid 1960s** and first used in 1966, so it would fall between mainframe computers (1946) and personal computers (1975) in our timeline.

So we might need:
- **The Computer** (Mainframe, ~1946) - position 26  
- **Integrated Circuit Computers** (like Apollo Guidance Computer, ~1960s) - new position around 28-29
- **Personal Computers** (~1975-1981) - position 32-33

I'd need to see your current project structure to give you a specific answer about why login isn't in `app/(admin)/admin`. This could be intentional design or something that needs to be moved.

Here are the most common reasons login might be located elsewhere:

**Shared Login Pattern** - Login is often placed at the root level (like `app/login` or `app/auth/login`) because the same login form serves multiple user types (admin, regular users, etc.)

**Route Group Structure** - In Next.js, if you're using route groups like `(admin)`, the login might be outside because:
- Users need to authenticate *before* accessing the admin section
- The admin route group might have middleware that requires authentication

**Authentication Flow** - Login typically happens before route protection, so it's common to have:
```
app/
  login/          <- General login
  (admin)/
    admin/        <- Protected admin routes
    dashboard/
```

**Access Control** - Login might be at a higher level to handle redirects to different areas based on user roles.

Could you share your current folder structure? That would help me understand whether this is the intended design or if moving login to `app/(admin)/admin` would make sense for your specific use case.

Also, are you using any specific authentication library (NextAuth, Clerk, etc.) or route protection middleware? That context would help explain the current setup.

Looking at your structure, the login placement in `app/(admin)/admin/login` is actually **correct and well-organized**! Here's why this makes sense:

## Why This Structure Works Well

**Route Group Organization** - Your `(admin)` route group contains all admin-related functionality, including authentication. This keeps admin concerns separated from your public site.

**Clean URLs** - This gives you `/admin/login` which is intuitive and clearly indicates it's for admin access.

**Logical Grouping** - Everything admin-related (login, dashboard, scripts) is contained within the same route group, making it easier to apply consistent layouts and middleware.

**NextAuth Integration** - Your auth API is at `api/auth/[...nextauth]` which can handle authentication for both admin and regular users, while the login UI is appropriately placed in the admin section.

## Your Current Flow Likely Works Like:
1. User goes to `/admin/login` 
2. Authenticates via NextAuth API
3. Gets redirected to `/admin/dashboard` or `/admin`
4. Middleware probably protects the `/admin/*` routes

## Alternative Approaches (but yours is fine):
Some developers put login at the root level when they have multiple user types, but since you have a clear site/admin separation with route groups, your current structure is actually quite clean.

**The real question is**: Are you experiencing any issues with this structure, or were you just wondering about best practices? Your current setup follows Next.js App Router conventions well and keeps things organized.

If you're having specific issues with authentication flow or routing, I'd be happy to help troubleshoot those!

For a CMS/page builder, I'd recommend creating a dedicated top-level `/editor` folder rather than keeping it in `/components`. Here's why and how:

## Recommended Structure

```
/
├── editor/
│   ├── components/
│   │   ├── BlockEditor.tsx
│   │   ├── ComponentPalette.tsx  
│   │   ├── PageEditor.tsx
│   │   └── PropertyEditor.tsx
│   ├── blocks/
│   │   └── customBlocks.ts
│   ├── lib/
│   │   └── componentLibrary.ts
│   └── types/
│       └── editor.ts
├── components/  (keep for general UI)
├── app/
└── ...
```

## Why This Makes Sense

**Domain Separation** - The editor is a distinct feature domain, not just UI components
**Future Growth** - CMSs tend to expand with more editor logic, configs, block definitions, etc.
**Import Clarity** - `import from '@/editor/components/BlockEditor'` vs `import from '@/components/BlockEditor'` makes the purpose clearer
**Team Collaboration** - Easier for team members to understand what's editor-specific vs general app components

components/
├── editor/
│   ├── BlockEditor.tsx
│   ├── ComponentPalette.tsx
│   └── ...
├── ui/
└── layout/
```

The top-level `/editor` approach is probably better long-term since CMS/page builders often become substantial parts of the codebase with their own routing, APIs, and complex state management.

Sponsored Top-Level Domains (sTLDs): These TLDs are sponsored by organisations and are intended for particular communities or groups.Examples include .aero for the aviation industry, .museum for museums and .edu for educational institutions. Infrastructure Top-Level Domains (iTLDs): These TLDs are intended for use by the infrastructure of the internet, such as .arpa and .int.

It is a specialized domain extension managed by the Registry, iSelect Ltd, and it's intended for websites that offer comparison shopping or services, providing users with an easily recognizable and credible platform to comparison services.

The .compare domain extension is ideal for businesses that offer comparison-based services or products, such as price comparison websites, review platforms, or comparison-driven e-commerce businesses. A domain extension or TLD (Top-Level Domain) is the final part of your domain name. For example, in domainwheel.com, the TLD is .com. Domain extensions are intended to categorize your website. Some have highly specific uses, like .edu for educational organizations, while others like .com can be used for any type of website.

The next thing we’ll look at for our Namecheap vs Porkbun comparison is how easy it is to register a domain with each company. Let’s start with Porkbun. You can start by going to the Porkbun website, typing your ideal domain into the search bar, and clicking on the magnifying glass. This will take you to a page where you’ll see availability for your ideal domain/TLD, plus alternate TLDs available for your desired domain. The one drawback of this search is that the top TLDs listed, other than the one you searched for, aren’t very common. Of the most common TLDs, only .org is immediately visible, and it’s not actually part of the main list. If you want to get a .net domain, you’ll need to run an entirely separate search. On the other hand, you’ll notice my favorite thing about Porkbun’s purchase process as soon as you click the + button next to your chosen domain: there’s no upsell.

This takes you to a page where you can see the availability of your ideal domain. Just like with Porkbun, you’ll also see other TLDs that are available. The main difference vs Porkbun though, is that Namecheap will also show you more commonly used TLDs like .org and .net. You can buy as many of these domains as you want by clicking the Add to cart button next to every domain you’re interested in. Clicking on the Add to cart button opens an upsell box, where Namecheap encourages you to buy services like web and email hosting: This is kind of annoying, but it’s easy enough to move past.

Both registrars make it quite simple to buy a domain. The difference is that Porkbun isn’t as pushy with its upsells, which can be annoying if you’re certain you only want a domain name. input.content:
# Hotel Updates Management - Power App Conversion Guide ## Overview This guide will help you convert the HTML-based Hotel Updates Management system into a Microsoft Power App with the same functionality and improved features. ## 1. Data Source Setup ### Option A: SharePoint List (Recommended) Create a SharePoint list named **"HotelUpdates"** with these columns: | Column Name | Type | Settings | |-------------|------|----------| | Title | Single line of text | Default SharePoint column | | Hotel | Choice | Grand Plaza, Ocean View Resort, City Center Inn, Mountain Lodge, Sunset Beach Hotel | | UpdateType | Choice | Promotion, Restriction, Hotel Change, Booking Instruction | | UpdateDate | Date and time | Date only | | Content | Multiple lines of text | Plain text, enhanced rich text | | Created | Date and time | Automatic | | Modified | Date and time | Automatic | ### Option B: Dataverse Table Create a custom table with the same structure if you prefer Dataverse. ## 2. Power App Structure ### Screen Layout - **Main Screen**: Hotel Updates Dashboard - **Form Screen**: Add/Edit Updates (optional - can use forms on main screen) ### Key Components #### 2.1 Header Section - **Label**: "Hotel Updates Management" - **Subtitle**: "Stay informed with the latest hotel information" - **Background**: Gradient using Power Apps theming #### 2.2 Filter Controls Container Create a horizontal container with these controls: **Hotel Filter Dropdown** ```powerapp Items: ["All Hotels", "Grand Plaza", "Ocean View Resort", "City Center Inn", "Mountain Lodge", "Sunset Beach Hotel"] Default: "All Hotels" ``` **Date From Picker** ```powerapp Default: Today() - 7 ``` **Date To Picker** ```powerapp Default: Today() ``` **Results Count Dropdown** ```powerapp Items: [3, 5, 7, 10] Default: 5 ``` **Admin Mode Toggle** ```powerapp Default: false Text: "Admin Mode" ``` #### 2.3 Gallery Control (Updates Display) **Gallery Items Formula** ```powerapp SortByColumns( Filter( HotelUpdates, And( Or( DropdownHotelFilter.Selected.Value = "All Hotels", Hotel.Value = DropdownHotelFilter.Selected.Value ), UpdateDate >= DatePickerFrom.SelectedDate, UpdateDate <= DatePickerTo.SelectedDate ) ), "UpdateDate", Descending ) ``` **Gallery Template Structure:** - Container with card-like appearance - Update type badge with conditional formatting - Hotel name (prominent) - Date display - Content text - Admin buttons (visible when admin mode is on) #### 2.4 Form Controls **Add/Edit Form** ```powerapp DataSource: HotelUpdates Item: If(IsBlank(SelectedUpdate), Defaults(HotelUpdates), SelectedUpdate) ``` ## 3. Key Formulas and Logic ### 3.1 Update Type Color Coding ```powerapp // In a label or container for update type badge Fill: Switch( ThisItem.UpdateType.Value, "Promotion", RGBA(232, 245, 232, 1), "Restriction", RGBA(255, 234, 167, 1), "Hotel Change", RGBA(221, 214, 254, 1), "Booking Instruction", RGBA(227, 242, 253, 1), RGBA(248, 249, 250, 1) ) Color: Switch( ThisItem.UpdateType.Value, "Promotion", RGBA(39, 174, 96, 1), "Restriction", RGBA(225, 112, 85, 1), "Hotel Change", RGBA(124, 58, 237, 1), "Booking Instruction", RGBA(25, 118, 210, 1), RGBA(108, 117, 125, 1) ) ``` ### 3.2 Admin Mode Visibility ```powerapp // For edit/delete buttons Visible: ToggleAdminMode.Value ``` ### 3.3 Results Counter ```powerapp // Label showing count Text: "Showing " & CountRows(GalleryUpdates.AllItems) & " update" & If(CountRows(GalleryUpdates.AllItems) <> 1, "s", "") ``` ### 3.4 Form Validation ```powerapp // Save button DisplayMode DisplayMode: If( And( Not(IsBlank(ComboBoxHotel.Selected)), Not(IsBlank(ComboBoxUpdateType.Selected)), Not(IsBlank(DatePickerUpdate.SelectedDate)), Not(IsBlank(TextAreaContent.Text)) ), DisplayMode.Edit, DisplayMode.Disabled ) ``` ## 4. Enhanced Power Apps Features ### 4.1 Responsive Design - Use responsive containers - Set breakpoints for mobile/tablet/desktop - Implement collapsible filter panel on mobile ### 4.2 Offline Capabilities ```powerapp // On app start, cache data for offline use OnStart: ClearCollect( CachedUpdates, HotelUpdates ); ``` ### 4.3 Search Functionality Add a text input for content search: ```powerapp Filter( HotelUpdates, And( // ... existing filters ... Or( IsBlank(TextInputSearch.Text), TextInputSearch.Text in Content, TextInputSearch.Text in Hotel.Value ) ) ) ``` ### 4.4 Export to Excel ```powerapp // Button OnSelect Export( GalleryUpdates.AllItems, "HotelUpdates_" & Text(Today(), "yyyy-mm-dd") ) ``` ### 4.5 Email Notifications ```powerapp // Send email when new update is created Office365Outlook.SendEmailV2( "hotelmanager@company.com", "New Hotel Update: " & ComboBoxHotel.Selected.Value, "A new " & ComboBoxUpdateType.Selected.Value & " update has been added for " & ComboBoxHotel.Selected.Value & ".

" & TextAreaContent.Text ) ``` ## 5. Power Automate Integration ### Flow 1: Daily Update Summary - **Trigger**: Recurrence (daily) - **Action**: Get items from SharePoint where UpdateDate = today - **Action**: Send email summary to stakeholders ### Flow 2: Approval Workflow - **Trigger**: When item is created in SharePoint - **Action**: Start approval process - **Action**: Update item status based on approval ## 6. Security and Permissions ### SharePoint Permissions - **Readers**: Can view all updates - **Contributors**: Can add/edit updates (admin mode) - **Owners**: Full control ### Power Apps Security ```powerapp // Admin mode visibility based on user ToggleAdminMode.Visible: User().Email in ["admin1@company.com", "admin2@company.com"] ``` ## 7. Performance Optimization ### 7.1 Delegation - Use delegable functions in gallery filters - Limit gallery items to 500 or use pagination - Use Search() function for text searches ### 7.2 Loading Performance ```powerapp // Show loading spinner LoadingSpinner.Visible: GalleryUpdates.Loading ``` ## 8. Testing Checklist - [ ] All filters work correctly - [ ] Admin mode shows/hides controls properly - [ ] Forms validate input correctly - [ ] Responsive design works on all screen sizes - [ ] Data saves and loads correctly - [ ] Performance is acceptable with large datasets - [ ] Permissions work as expected ## 9. Deployment Steps 1. **Create SharePoint list** with required columns 2. **Build Power App** following the structure above 3. **Test thoroughly** with sample data 4. **Set up Power Automate flows** (if needed) 5. **Configure security** and permissions 6. **Deploy to production** environment 7. **Train users** on new functionality ## 10. Advanced Features (Optional) ### Push Notifications - Integrate with Power Apps notification service - Send alerts for urgent updates ### Power BI Integration - Create dashboard for update analytics - Track update trends by hotel/type ### Teams Integration - Embed Power App in Teams - Send updates to Teams channels ### AI Builder Integration - Sentiment analysis on update content - Auto-categorization of updates This Power App will provide all the functionality of your HTML application with additional enterprise features like offline capability, mobile responsiveness, security, and integration with the Microsoft ecosystem.

## Fix the HTML Display Issue

### Step 1: Format the Rich Text Content
1. **Click on your gallery** to select it
2. **Click on the label** inside the gallery that's showing the HTML code (it's probably showing the Content field)
3. Look at the **Properties panel** on the right
4. Find the **"Text"** property
5. It probably shows something like: `ThisItem.Content`

### Step 2: Use the PlainText Function
1. **Replace** the Text property with:
   ```
   PlainText(ThisItem.Content)
   ```
2. Press **Enter**

This will strip out all the HTML formatting and show just the clean text.

### Step 3: Alternative - Keep Some Formatting
If you want to keep some of the rich text formatting (like bold, italics), you can use:
```
ThisItem.Content.PlainText
```

### Step 4: Test It
Your content should now show as clean, readable text instead of HTML code.

**Try this and let me know:**
- Does the text now display properly without HTML tags?
- Can you see your hotel update content clearly?

## Fix the Filter Height Issue

### Step 1: Create a Container for Filters
1. **Select all your filter controls** (Hotel dropdown, date pickers, Max Results dropdown)
2. Go to **Insert** → **"Container"** → **"Container"**
3. **Move all the filter controls into this container**

### Step 2: Set Container Properties
1. **Select the container**
2. In **Properties panel**, set:
   - **Height**: Fixed value like `80` or `100`
   - **Flexible height**: **Turn OFF** (uncheck)
   - **Direction**: **Horizontal**
   - **Wrap**: **Turn OFF** (uncheck)

### Step 3: Fix Individual Control Heights
For each filter control (dropdowns, date pickers):

1. **Select each control one by one**
2. Set **Height** to a fixed value like `40` or `50`
3. Set **AutoHeight**: **Turn OFF**

### Step 4: Alternative - Use Advanced Properties
1. **Select your container**
2. In the **formula bar**, change to **"LayoutMode"**
3. Set it to: `LayoutMode.Absolute`
4. This gives you more precise control over positioning

### Step 5: Test Responsive Behavior
1. **Preview your app** (F5 key)
2. Try resizing the browser window
3. The filter area should now stay a consistent height

**Which method would you like to try first?** The container approach usually works best for keeping consistent heights across different screen sizes.

chat_messages.text:
Great question! **FirstN** is a Power Apps function that limits how many records are returned.

## What FirstN Does

**FirstN** takes the first "N" number of items from a list/table.

**Syntax:**
```
FirstN(Table, NumberOfRecords)
```

## In Your Hotel App Context

```
FirstN(
    Filter(...),           // Your filtered hotel updates
    Value(ddMaxResults.Selected.Value)  // Number from dropdown (3, 5, 7, or 10)
)
```

**What this means:**
- If user selects "5" in Max Results dropdown → Show first 5 updates
- If user selects "10" in Max Results dropdown → Show first 10 updates

## Example
If you have 20 hotel updates total:
- `FirstN(HotelUpdates, 3)` = Shows only the first 3 updates
- `FirstN(HotelUpdates, 10)` = Shows only the first 10 updates

## Why We Use It
Without FirstN, your gallery would show ALL matching updates (could be hundreds). FirstN limits it to just the number the user wants to see.

**Alternative:** If you don't want the limit feature, you can remove FirstN and just use:
```
Filter(HotelUpdates, ...)
```

Does that make sense? Do you want to keep the max results limit or remove it?

## Solution: Move the π Outside the HTML Text Area

### Option 1: Position π in Header Area
1. Make sure your **π label is positioned in the blue header section** (not over the HTML text area)
2. The header should be a separate container/rectangle from your gallery area

### Option 2: Change the HTML Text to Regular Label
If you need the π in the content area:
1. **Select the HTML text control** that's blocking it
2. **Right-click** → **Send to back** 
3. Or **Select the π label** → **Right-click** → **Bring to front**

### Option 3: Use Z-Order in Advanced Properties
1. **Select the π label**
2. In **Advanced properties**, look for **ZIndex**
3. Set it to a **higher number** (like `10` or `100`)
4. **Select the HTML text**
5. Set its **ZIndex** to a **lower number** (like `1`)

### Option 4: Move to Container
1. **Create a container** for your header
2. **Put the π inside that container**
3. Keep HTML text controls in the main content area

**Which approach do you want to try?** The easiest is usually making sure the π is in the header area, not overlapping with HTML text controls.

chat_messages.text:
Good catch! The delegation warning means CountRows won't work efficiently with large datasets. Let's fix this with a delegable approach.

## Fix: Use LookUp Instead of CountRows

1. **Select your π label**
2. **Replace the OnSelect** with this delegable formula:
```
If(
    !IsBlank(LookUp(HotelUpdatesAdmin, AdminEmail = User().Email)),
    Set(IsAdminMode, !IsAdminMode);
    Notify("Admin mode " & If(IsAdminMode, "activated", "deactivated"), NotificationType.Success),
    Notify("Access denied - Admin privileges required", NotificationType.Error)
)
```

## How This Works
- **LookUp** is delegable (works with large datasets)
- **LookUp** returns the matching record or Blank() if not found
- **!IsBlank()** checks if a record was found
- No delegation warning!

## Alternative: Use Any Function
If you prefer, you can also use:
```

content.text: should the git repository on my computer and the folder for my server be different

chat_messages.text:
Yes, it's generally a best practice to keep your Git repository and your server deployment folder separate. Here's why and how to approach this:

### Why Keep Them Separate

1. **Deployment Security**: Your Git repository contains development history, potentially including sensitive information in previous commits that you wouldn't want accessible on the server.

2. **Performance**: Git repositories include the entire project history and metadata in the `.git` folder, which takes up disk space and isn't needed for running your application.

3. **Clean Environment**: Production servers should only contain what's necessary to run the application, without development artifacts.

4. **Reduced Attack Surface**: Exposing Git metadata could reveal information helpful for potential attackers.

5. **Deployment Control**: Separating concerns gives you more control over what gets deployed and when.

### Recommended Approach

**For Development**:
- Work in your local Git repository
- Commit changes, manage branches, etc.

**For Deployment**:
- Use a deployment pipeline that builds from your Git repository but deploys only the necessary files
- Alternatively, use a deployment strategy that pulls from Git but excludes the `.git` directory

### Common Deployment Methods

1. **Automated CI/CD**:
   - GitHub Actions, Jenkins, CircleCI, etc.
   - Build your application in the pipeline
   - Deploy only build artifacts to your server

2. **Manual but Structured**:
   - Use tools like `rsync` that can exclude the `.git` directory
   ```
   rsync -avz --exclude='.git/' /path/to/local/repo/ user@server:/path/to/deployment/
   ```

3. **Git-based with cleaning**:
   - Use Git to pull on your server but in a separate directory
   - Copy or link only production files to your server directory

4. **Container-based**:
   - Use Docker to build images from your repository
   - Deploy containers to your server

This separation creates a cleaner, more secure, and more maintainable deployment process.

That's a valid concern. Having to manually copy files would be inefficient and error-prone. Here are better approaches that maintain separation without requiring constant manual copying:

### Automated Solutions

1. **Continuous Deployment Pipeline**
   - Set up a simple CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, etc.)
   - It automatically deploys whenever you push to your main branch
   - No manual copying needed - just commit and push

2. **Git Hooks**
   - Create a post-commit or post-push hook that automatically deploys changes
   - Example script that runs after each commit:
   ```bash
   #!/bin/bash
   rsync -avz --exclude='.git/' --exclude='node_modules/' /path/to/repo/ /path/to/server/
   ```

3. **Watch Scripts**
   - Use tools like `nodemon` or simple bash scripts that watch for changes
   - Automatically sync when files change

4. **Deployment Tools**
   - Tools like PM2 for Node.js can handle deployment from Git
   - `pm2 deploy` can pull from your repository and restart your application

5. **Scripted Deployment**
   - Create a simple script you run manually when ready to deploy:
   ```bash
   ./deploy.sh
   ```
   - Inside the script, handle all copying/syncing operations

### Middle-Ground Approach

If you want something simpler but still maintaining separation:

- Keep your development Git repository in one folder
- Have your server folder elsewhere
- Use a simple script or command alias that you run when ready to deploy:

```bash
# Simple deploy script
rsync -avz --exclude='.git/' --exclude='node_modules/' --exclude='.env' ~/myproject/ ~/server/myproject/
ssh myserver "cd ~/server/myproject && npm install --production && pm2 restart app"
```

This way, you maintain separation for security and cleanliness but minimize the friction of deployment to a single command.

Which approach would work best with your current workflow?

chat_messages.text:
If you don't want separation between your Git repository and server folder, that's also a valid approach for certain scenarios. Here's how to make that work effectively:

### Direct Development/Deployment Approach

1. **Single Directory Setup**
   - Your Git repository is your server directory
   - You develop directly in the production environment (or pull changes directly into it)

2. **Benefits**
   - Simplicity - no need to copy or sync files
   - Immediate deployment - changes are immediately available
   - What you see is what you get - direct testing in the actual environment

3. **Important Considerations**

   - **Environment Variables**: Use `.env` files that are gitignored but present in your server directory
   ```
   # In production
   cp .env.example .env
   # Then edit .env with production values
   ```

   - **Git Security**: Ensure your `.git` directory isn't web-accessible
   ```
   # In Apache
   <DirectoryMatch "^/.*/\.git/">
     Order deny,allow
     Deny from all
   </DirectoryMatch>
   
   # In Nginx
   location ~ /\.git {
     deny all;
   }
   ```

   - **Branch Management**: Consider which branch is deployed
   ```bash
   # Stay on main/production branch on server
   git checkout main
   ```

   - **Node Modules**: You may want to run production installations
   ```bash
   npm install --production
   # or
   NODE_ENV=production npm install
   ```

   - **Build Process**: For compiled applications, run builds on the server
   ```bash
   npm run build
   ```

### How to Set It Up

```bash
# Initial setup on server
git clone your-repository.git /path/to/server
cd /path/to/server
npm install
npm run build # if needed
# Configure environment
cp .env.example .env
nano .env # edit with production values

# For updates
git pull
npm install # if dependencies changed
npm run build # if needed
# Restart service if needed
pm2 restart app # or similar
```

This approach works well for:
- Small projects or personal sites
- Development servers
- Situations where quick iteration is more important than strict environment separation

The main tradeoff is less separation between development and production, which could potentially lead to accidental exposure of development files or unintended changes going live immediately.

For connecting VSCode to GitHub, I recommend these extensions:

1. **GitHub Pull Requests and Issues** (Official Microsoft extension)
   - Handles PR reviews and issue management directly in VSCode
   - Allows you to create and review pull requests
   - Lets you browse and manage GitHub issues
   - Official extension from Microsoft/GitHub

2. **GitLens** (Most comprehensive)
   - Enhanced Git capabilities including blame annotations, code authorship
   - History and line-by-line git information
   - Repository/file/line history visualization
   - Works great with GitHub repositories

3. **GitHub Repositories** (For browsing without cloning)
   - Browse, search, edit, and commit to any GitHub repository directly
   - Work with repositories without having to clone them locally

1. Open VSCode
2. Click the Extensions icon in the sidebar (or press Ctrl+Shift+X)
3. Search for the extension name
4. Click "Install"

For basic GitHub integration, I'd start with the official "GitHub Pull Requests and Issues" extension. For more advanced features, add GitLens. If you need to browse repositories without cloning, add the GitHub Repositories extension.

Once installed, you'll need to authenticate by signing into your GitHub account when prompted by the extension.

content.title: How the GitHub CLI can now enable triangular workflows - The GitHub Blog
content.text:
Learn more about triangular workflows, how they work, and how to configure them for your Git workflows. See how you can leverage them on the GitHub CLI.

Most developers are familiar with the standard Git workflow. You create a branch, make changes, and push those changes back to the same branch on the main repository. Git calls this a centralized workflow. It’s straightforward and works well for many projects. However, sometimes you might want to pull changes from a different branch directly into your feature branch to help you keep your branch updated without constantly needing to merge or rebase. However, you’ll still want to push local changes to your own branch. This is where triangular workflows come in. It’s possible that some of you have already used triangular workflows, even without knowing it. When you fork a repo, contribute to your fork, then open a pull request back to the original repo, you’re working in a triangular workflow. While this can work seamlessly on github.com, the process hasn’t always been seamless with the GitHub CLI.

To provide a framework for what we set out to do, it’s important to first understand some Git basics. Git, at its core, is a way to store and catalog changes on a repository and communicate those changes between copies of that repository. This workflow typically looks like the diagram below: ... The building blocks of this diagram illustrate two important Git concepts you likely use every day, a ref and push/pull. A ref is a reference to a repository and branch. It has two parts: the remote, usually a name like origin or upstream, and the branch. If the remote is the local repository, it is blank. So, in the example above, origin/branch in the purple box is a remote ref, referring to a branch named branch on the repository name origin, while branch in the green box is a local ref, referring to a branch named branch on the local machine. While working with GitHub, the remote ref is usually the repository you are hosting on GitHub.

In contrast, a triangular workflow pushes to and pulls from different refs. A common use case for this configuration is to pull directly from a remote repository’s default branch into your local feature branch, eliminating the need to run commands like git rebase <default> or git merge <default> on your feature branch to ensure the branch you’re working on is always up to date with the default branch. However, when pushing changes, this configuration will typically push to a remote ref with the same branch name as the feature branch. Figure 4: juxtaposing centralized workflows from triangular workflows. We complete the triangle when considering pull requests: the headRef is the pushRef for the local ref and the baseRef is the pullRef for the local branch: ... We can go one step further and set up triangular workflows using different remotes as well.

Some commands in gh are opinionated about remote names and will resolve remotes in this order: upstream, github, origin, <other remotes unstably sorted>. There is a convenience command you can run to supersede this:* gh repo set-default [<repository>] to override the default behavior above and preferentially resolve <repository> as the default remote repo. ↩ · If you find a git configuration that doesn’t work, please open an issue in the OSS repo so we can fix it. ↩ ... content.text:
Infosec in Brief: Also, phone cleaner apps are a data-sucking scam, Singapore considering the literal rod for scammers, and more

Infosec in Brief Microsoft has spotted a malvertising campaign that downloaded nastyware hosted on GitHub and exposed nearly a million devices to information thieves. Discovered by Microsoft Threat Intelligence late last year, the campaign saw pirate vid-streaming websites embed malvertising redirectors to generate pay-per-view or pay-per-click revenue from malvertising platforms. “These redirectors subsequently routed traffic through one or two additional malicious redirectors, ultimately leading to another website, such as a malware or tech support scam website, which then redirected to GitHub,” according to Microsoft’s threat research team. GitHub hosted a first-stage payload that installed code that dropped two other payloads. One gathered system configuration info such as data on memory size, graphics capabilities, screen resolution, the operating system present, and user paths.

The attackers built four to five redirect layers in the campaign, each of which followed on from the GitHub dropper to install more nastiness that it appears were designed to steal information including stored browser credentials. Microsoft noted that the malicious repos have since been taken down, and provided plenty of indicators of compromise and other valuable information in its report to aid in hunting down and stopping related campaigns. Future open-source software vulnerabilities might come with a fedora, as Red Hat is now a CVE numbering authority of last resort. content.title: What's inside an RPM .repo file? | Red Hat Developer
content.text:
A .repo file is the key to package management on Red Hat-derived Linux distros. Take a look inside to see how they work

The previous article in this series, How does RPM package discovery work?, described how the RPM package management technology discovers and installs an .rpm package on a local computer running the

The structure of a .repo file is predefined according to specification. Table 1 is a list of the more common fields defined in the specification. As noted, when you run dnf install, the command will inspect the .repo files in the /etc/yum.repos.d directory to locate an appropriate repository. Once the repository is located, dnf install will execute according to the parameters defined as fields in the given .repo file. You can learn about all the specified fields for a .repo file by reading the dnf documentation. The information in a .repo file is used not only to populate available packages using dnf install but also as the source of data for the dnf repolist command, which informs the system which repositories are enabled. The listing below shows a list of repositories returned when executing the command dnf repolist. The listing has two column headings, repo id and repo name.

$ rpm -q -i jq Name : jq Version : 1.6 Release : 9.el9 Architecture: x86_64 Install Date: Mon 30 May 2022 02:07:40 PM PDT Group : Unspecified Size : 400049 License : MIT and ASL 2.0 and CC-BY and GPLv3 Signature : RSA/SHA256, Wed 11 Aug 2021 05:50:53 PM PDT, Key ID 05b555b38483c65d Source RPM : jq-1.6-9.el9.src.rpm Build Date : Mon 09 Aug 2021 03:22:17 PM PDT Build Host : x86-02.stream.rdu2.redhat.com Packager : builder@centos.org Vendor : CentOS URL : http://stedolan.github.io/jq/ Summary : Command-line JSON processor Description : lightweight and flexible command-line JSON processor jq is like sed for JSON data – you can use it to slice and filter and map and transform structured data with the same ease that sed, awk, grep and friends let you play with text. It is written in portable C, and it has zero runtime dependencies. jq can mangle the data format that you have into the one that you want with very little effort, and the program to do so is often shorter and simpler than you'd e

An interesting point to note is that values for the repo IDs and names are extracted directly from the .repo file for the corresponding repository—fedora.repo, in this case. For example, when you look back to the first listing above, you'll see that the .repo file has the following in the first two lines of content: ... The dnf repolist command extracts the value fedora from the [fedora] entry in the file fedora.repo. The value for the repo name, Fedora 35 - x86_64 is extracted from the name field of the .repo file, which is declared as Fedora $releasever - $basearch. At this point, you may be wondering: how does the string Fedora $releasever - $basearch transform into Fedora 35 - x86_64? As it happens, $releasever and $basearch are variables that get resolved at runtime. And how are their values determined? Well, to determine the value of $releasever variable, check the /etc/fedora-release file.

content.title: Terraform Files - How to Structure Terraform Project
content.text:
Learn how to structure your Terraform files in an efficient and standardized way that makes it easier to scale your projects in the future.

As exciting as starting a new Terraform project may sound, the first question is where and how we begin. What should be the first file that needs to be created? When the project grows, we realize a few things and learn our lessons about structuring a project in a certain way, but it is too late to put in refactoring efforts. Various aspects influence the way we manage our Terraform config in a repository. In this post, we will learn about them and discuss a few important strategies and best practices around structuring Terraform project files in an efficient and standardized way. ... Terraform configuration files are used for writing your Terraform code. They have a .tf extension and use a declarative language called HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) to describe the different components that are used to automate your infrastructure. Terraform should always be used with a version control system, so all of your Terraform files should be stored inside it.

README.md — As a general best practice, every repository should contain a README.md file that includes an overview of the source code, usage instructions, and any other relevant and important information · Automation scripts — When there is a need to include automation scripts (bash, shell, python, golang, etc.) in CI/CD workflow, when certain scripts are required to be executed on the target resource being created, or to build a source code, etc. Bash/shell scripts are very powerful in general; there are many reasons to use them. YAMLs — The most common usage of YAML files in Terraform in this context is when implementing CI/CD automation. Since we are discussing the Terraform project structure, the .gitignore file plays a special role. As observed in previous sections, a Terraform project consists of multiple kinds of files and binaries. For several reasons, not all files and directories should be part of the git repository.

However, this simple structure may not be enough for larger projects. Modules are a great way to follow the DRY principle when working with Terraform Infrastructure as Code. Modules encapsulate a set of Terraform config files created to serve a specific purpose. As discussed earlier, we may slice and group the infrastructure based on the type of components or the service they support. In the diagram below, the Terraform project uses two modules to help create VPCs and Databases. These modules are reusable and based on the types of components. Thus, it becomes easy to plug them into other Terraform projects. The project root directory contains its set of Terraform config files. These config files also declare module blocks in addition to the general resource blocks. The module blocks refer to the source of these modules — it could be a remote git repository, Terraform Registry, or a locally developed module.

The project directory structure after initialization is shown below: Do not get confused about the additional files included in the .terraform directory. They belong to the VPC module we used in our main.tf file. This is to show how modules are managed internally. If customization is needed, it is possible to do the same here. Technically, we can now apply these changes, and a VPC will be created and managed in the state file of our project, i.e., in the project root directory. It is possible for modules to have nested modules. Also, note that all the additional files related to VPC modules downloaded in the “.terraform” directory are “gitignored” by default, so they will never be pushed to the repository. When creating your Terraform configuration, you can either structure your projects using monorepos, or polyrepos. You may even find examples in which engineers are using monorepos for their modules and polyrepos for their environments or the other way around.

content.title: Files Deleted From GitHub Repos Leak Valuable Secrets - SecurityWeek
content.text:
A security researcher has discovered hundreds of leaked secrets by restoring files deleted from GitHub repositories.

The issue his research brings to the spotlight is that developers may not be aware that Git retains copies of all files within a repository, even if they are no longer available in the working directory. A distributed revision control system, Git tracks content using a commit – tree – blob structure. It captures snapshots of the repository’s state, and relies on branches for reviewing commit history, and on tags for referencing specific commits. Because it stores each version of a file as a unique object and keeps a complete history of the changes made to a repository, Git makes it easy to revert to previous states and to restore files that have been deleted or removed from the working directory and committed. “Once a commit is created, its data is stored in .git/objects and remains there even if it’s no longer referenced by any branch or tag.

“To completely remove a file from history, one must rewrite history using tools like git filter-branch, git-filter-repo or by manually rebasing and running garbage collector (with prune) to clear unreachable objects,” Brizinov says. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. When it comes to public repositories, he notes, completely removing committed files is virtually impossible, as they may have been copied or cloned elsewhere. To shed light on these risks, Brizinov built an automated tool to clone public repositories, traverse all commits to find deleted files, restore them, and scan them for secrets such as API keys, tokens, and credentials. He focused on companies with active bug bounty programs and those with Github repositories that have over 5,000 stars, and discovered hundreds of active secrets, mainly in binary files that had been deleted after being committed to the repository.

In this structure, we see this reflected by having a data/ folder (a source), a folder for the code that performs the operations (src/) and a place to put the results (output/). The root analysis file (the sole R file on the top level) is responsible for launching and orchestrating the functions defined in the src/ folder’s contents. The data folder is, unsurprisingly, where your data goes. In many cases, you may not have any file-formatted raw data (e.g. where the raw data is accessed via a *DBC connection to a database), and you might even keep all intermediate files there, although that’s pretty uncommon on the whole, and might not make you the local DBA’s favourite (not to mention data protection issues). So while the raw/ subfolder might be dispensed with, you’ll most definitely need a data/ folder. When it comes to data, it is crucial to make a distinction between source data and generated data.

The library model: in this case, the root folder of src/ holds individual .R scripts that when executed will carry out an analysis. There may be one or more such scripts, e.g. for different analyses or different depths of insight. Subfolders of src/ are named after the kind of scripts they contain, e.g. ETL, transformation, plotting. The risk with this structure is that sometimes it’s tricky to remember what’s where, so descriptive file names are particularly important. The pipeline model: in this case, there is a main runner script or potentially a small number. These go through scripts in a sequence. It is a sensible idea in such a case to establish sequential subfolders or sequentially numbered scripts that are executed in sequence. Typically, this model performs better if there are at most a handful distinct pipelines. Whichever approach you adopt, a crucial point is to keep function definition and application separate.

This page provides an overview of all the folder and file conventions in Next.js, and recommendations for organizing your project. Top-level folders are used to organize your application's code and static assets. Top-level files are used to configure your application, manage dependencies, run middleware, integrate monitoring tools, and define environment variables. Next.js is unopinionated about how you organize and colocate your project files. But it does provide several features to help you organize your project. The components defined in special files are rendered in a specific hierarchy: ... In the app directory, nested folders define route structure. Each folder represents a route segment that is mapped to a corresponding segment in a URL path.

Next.js supports storing application code (including app) inside an optional src folder. This separates application code from project configuration files which mostly live in the root of a project. content.title: Next.js - Wikipedia
content.text:
Next.js is an open-source web development framework created by the private company Vercel providing React-based web applications with server-side rendering and static rendering. React documentation mentions Next.js among "Recommended Toolchains" advising it to developers when "building a server-rendered website with Node.js". Where traditional React apps can only render their content in the client-side browser, Next.js extends this functionality to include applications rendered on the server-side. The copyright and trademarks for Next.js are owned by Vercel, which also maintains and leads its 

Next.js was first released as an open-source project on GitHub on October 25, 2016. It was originally developed based on six principles: out-of-the-box functionality requiring no setup, JavaScript everywhere, all functions are written in JavaScript, automatic code-splitting and server-rendering, configurable data-fetching, anticipating requests, and simplifying deployment. Next.js 2.0 was announced in March 2017 including several improvements that made it easier to work with small websites. It also increased the build efficiency and improved the scalability of the hot-module replacement feature. Version 7.0 was released in September 2018 with improved error handling and support for React's context API for improved dynamic route handling. This was also the first version to upgrade to Webpack 4. Version 8.0 was released in February 2019 and was the first version to offer serverless deployment of applications, in which the code is split up into lambda functions that are run on demand.

Next.js supports styling with CSS as well as precompiled Scss and Sass, CSS-in-JS, and styled JSX. In addition, it is built with TypeScript support and smart bundling. The open-source transpiler SWC is used to transform and compile code into JavaScript usable by a browser. Webpack, another open-source tool, is used to bundle the modules afterward, however it is currently being replaced with TurboPack. All of these tools are used with npm in a terminal. The main feature of Next.js is its use of server-side rendering to reduce the burden on web browsers and provide enhanced security. This can be done for any part of the application or the entire system, allowing for content-rich pages to be singled out for server-side rendering. It can also be done only for first-time visitors, to reduce the burden on web browsers that have yet to download any of the site's assets.

The "hot reloading" feature detects changes as they are made and re-renders the appropriate pages so the server avoids the need to be restarted. This allows changes made to the application code to be immediately reflected in the web browser, though some browsers will require the page to be refreshed. The software uses page-based routing for developer convenience and includes support for dynamic routing. Other features include hot-module replacement so that modules can be replaced live, automatic code splitting, which only includes code necessary to load the page, and page prefetching to reduce load time. Next.js also supports Incremental Static Regeneration and static site generation - a compiled version of the website is usually built during build time and saved as a .next folder. When a user makes a request, the pre-built version which are static HTML pages are cached and sent to them.

Developers recognize several problems with this strategy however, such as not catering to users who do not have access to JavaScript or have disabled it, potential security issues, significantly extended page loading times, and harm to the site's overall search engine optimization. Frameworks such as Next.js sidestep these problems by allowing some or all of the website to be rendered on the server-side before being sent to the client. Next.js is one of the most popular frameworks for React. It is one of several recommended "toolchains" available when starting a new app, all of which provide a layer of abstraction to aid in common tasks. Next.js requires Node.js and can be initialized using npm. Google has contributed to the Next.js project, including 43 pull requests in 2019. As of October 2024, the framework is used by many large websites, including Walmart, Apple, Nike, Netflix, TikTok, Uber, Lyft, Starbucks and Spotify.
